agent_notes: challoti is the hardest word in the psalm. The commentaries offer: from חלה 'be sick' (my sickness, Rashi, Metzudat David), from חלל 'pierce/die' (Radak and Meiri, 'my dying'), from חיל 'trembling' (Metzudat Zion), and from חלה 'to entreat' by Ibn Ezra. shenot is read as 'years' (from שנה) or as 'change' (from שנה 'alter', Rashi, Metzudat David, Targum, Ibn Ezra's 'others'). KJV, ASV, Webster supply 'but I will remember' and read 'years', borrowing from v. 12; the Hebrew has no such verb. My literal layer keeps the fragment verbless; the dramatic layer chooses 'my sickness' and 'years' while keeping the ambiguity audible. The Radak reference reads 'shenit' for shenot; I took it as the same word.

Qere ezkor ('I will remember') against Ketiv ezkir ('I will mention / cause to be remembered'), as Radak reports. STEPBible follows the Qere and so do I. The shift from third person (Yah) to second person (your wonder) inside one verse is original, and I kept it.

The commentary and the dramatic layer both keep the sense 'turn over in thought', which is what Rashi, Radak and the Metzudot take, with the speaking sense carried by אשיחה.

agent_notes: Morphology gives zoremu as Pual (they were poured out), so 'clouds' can be the agent ('clouds poured out') or an apposition ('waters were poured out, clouds'). KJV, ASV and BBE all make clouds the subject. I follow that in the dramatic layer and keep the Hebrew order in the literal layer. Malbim's reading that God appeared to the waters as water is quoted only as his view.

The form חֲצָצֶיךָ is a rare doubled plural of 'arrow' (khets); Rashi says it equals חִצֶּיךָ. Radak and Meiri offer 'small stones / gravel' (khatsats) instead. I follow Rashi and Metzudat David in 'arrows' = lightning.

agent_notes: The cohortative forms (ezkerah, ve'ehemayah, 'asichah) are rendered as 'let me / I would'; KJV and Webster turn them into past narrative. 'ehemayah is the written yod-ending form of the root המה (Ibn Ezra, Radak), not a separate root.

שמורות עיני is read three ways in the commentaries: watches of the night (Radak, Meiri's second reading), eyelids held open (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Meiri's first reading), and eyelids held shut in stupor or near death (Rashi, Malbim, Meiri's second reading). The dramatic layer 'hold my eyelids open' is one choice among these, taken because the context (vv. 3-7: night, brooding, remembering) fits a sleepless vigil. The literal layer 'watches' keeps both the night-watch and the guard-of-the-eye senses.

STEPBible glosses שמרות as 'eyelids of'; I keep 'watches' in the gloss and literal layer because the word is plural feminine of the same root as the night 'watches' (אשמרות), and the sense is disputed.
